questions.question: How is the tool made and installed? steering.md settles neither the language the tool is written in nor how a newcomer gets it onto macOS and Linux, so the README's Requirements and Installation cannot say what must be in place or what to run, and the architecture (T2) must follow what the README says.
questions.recommended: A single Python 3 program using only the standard library, installed with `pipx install` from the organize-downloads folder of the GitHub repository lovaizu/playground, because Python 3 runs the same on macOS and Linux, needs nothing else installed, and its tests run by one command.

questions.question: Under which license is the tool offered, and where are fuller use and what changed in each version written? steering.md names neither, so the README's License, Documentation and Development sections cannot name a place the reader can reach.
questions.recommended: The MIT license (or the repository's own license, if it already has one), fuller use in organize-downloads/docs/usage.md and changes in organize-downloads/CHANGELOG.md, both added with the tool, and Development linking to organize-downloads/docs/architecture.md from T2, because each then is a page in the same repository the reader installs from.

answers.answer:
The user answered both questions on organize-downloads/README.md; each is kept as a decision of work t1.1.
1. How the tool is made and installed: The tool is one Python 3 program in a single file, using only Python's standard library; it is installed by downloading that file into ~/.local/bin and making it runnable, on macOS and Linux alike, with nothing else to install. Its tests run by one command with what Python itself provides. (Not pipx.)
2. License and the places of fuller use and of changes: The tool is offered under the MIT license, at organize-downloads/LICENSE. Fuller use is written in organize-downloads/docs/usage.md and the changes of each version in organize-downloads/CHANGELOG.md, both still to be made with the tool; the README's Development links to organize-downloads/docs/architecture.md, made by T2.

questions.question: The README's download address (README.md line 149, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lovaizu/playground/main/organize-downloads/organize-downloads) gives 404, because the tool's file organize-downloads/organize-downloads does not exist yet and the plan (steering.md Tasks) has no task that makes it and puts it on main. Until it is there, no reader can install the tool, run --help or the Example's three runs, so B-4 cannot be met from the README alone. Should a task making the tool at organize-downloads/organize-downloads be added to the plan, with the README's installation and Example run again by a first user once that file is on main?
questions.recommended: Yes: keep the address as decided, add to the plan a build task that makes the tool at organize-downloads/organize-downloads and merges it to main, and take B-4 as met only when a first user installs from that address and gets the Example's output, because the address can only work once the file is on main and no change to the README can make it work sooner.

questions.question: Of the four places Documentation, Development and License link to (README.md lines 159, 161, 165, 169), none is there yet: T2 makes organize-downloads/docs/architecture.md, but no task in the plan makes organize-downloads/docs/usage.md, organize-downloads/CHANGELOG.md or organize-downloads/LICENSE, so a reader would land on missing pages, including the license's full terms. Should these three files be added, and by which work?
questions.recommended: Add organize-downloads/LICENSE, with the standard MIT text and the copyright holder and year you name (such as lovaizu, 2026), as a file of this work t1.1 so it is there when the README is approved, and add to the plan tasks making organize-downloads/docs/usage.md and organize-downloads/CHANGELOG.md with the tool, because the license needs nothing from the tool while the usage page and the change list can only be written once the tool exists.

chosen.chosen: LICENSE holds the standard MIT text as the Open Source Initiative gives it, headed "MIT License", with only the decided copyright line filled in.
chosen.why: The decision names the MIT license and its copyright line; the standard text unchanged is what readers and tools recognise as MIT.

chosen.chosen: The download address is https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lovaizu/playground/main/organize-downloads/organize-downloads, the tool's single file named organize-downloads in the organize-downloads folder of main, fetched with curl.
chosen.why: The decision says the file is downloaded into ~/.local/bin; steering.md's pull request is in lovaizu/playground, a raw address on main serves the file as it is, and naming the file as the command means it runs by that name without renaming; curl is on macOS and most Linux systems.

chosen.chosen: Python 3.8 or later is the version the README asks for.
chosen.why: The decision says Python 3 with only its standard library and names no version; 3.8 sets a floor low enough for older systems still in use, which I have not checked against a list of systems, and the tool is to use nothing a later standard library alone gives.

chosen.chosen: The options are --move and --undo, with the folder given after the options and ~/Downloads when none is given, and each line's wording is as the Example shows ("name -> Folder/", "name: stays, <why>", "name: back from Folder/").
chosen.why: steering.md names an option that moves and one that undoes but not their names or the lines' wording; short words that say the action let the reader type them from memory, and the README is what the build and T2 make the tool to.

chosen.chosen: The full list of extensions of each kind is the table in the Example: the steering.md examples plus jpeg, heif, bmp, tif, tiff; doc, xls, ppt, odt, ods, odp, rtf, pages, numbers, key; tgz, bz2, xz; aac, flac, ogg, opus, aiff; avi, webm, m4v, matched in capitals or small letters alike by the part after the last dot.
chosen.why: AC2 leaves the full list to the design and T1 to hold it; these are the common files of each kind met in a Downloads folder on macOS and Linux, and matching the last dot gives archive.tar.gz to Archives with one rule.

chosen.chosen: The PATH line is added to ~/.zshrc on macOS and ~/.bashrc on Linux.
chosen.why: Those are the shells each system starts by default, so a newcomer with no setup of their own finds the line takes effect.

chosen.chosen: The first use tells macOS readers that macOS may ask whether the terminal may access the Downloads folder, and to allow it.
chosen.why: macOS guards the Downloads folder and asks the first time a terminal reads it; a reader who refuses gets no files listed and cannot tell why, and the README says "may" since a terminal already allowed is not asked.
